records.conclusion: Existing visa and capacity/training rules may supply the EU result for many ordinary removals; a different company-permit name is not itself a gap. A narrower residual survives because the visa expressly has removal-work exceptions, while the EU prior undertaking-permit duty has no corresponding low-intensity exception. Foreground this scope question and the substantial existing controls.
legalResult: New EU Article 15 requires a competent-authority permit before demolition/asbestos-removal work, supported by Article 6 compliance evidence and training certificates, and a public list. Article 2 sets 21 December 2025; the 2029 derogation concerns measurement/limits, not permits.
The fresh EU amendment narrows Article 3(3) low-intensity derogation to notification Article 4. It does not excuse Article 15 permission.

Existing Article 11(3) worksite visas are a credible form of prior authorisation. Article 11ter requires operational-capacity evidence before obtaining that visa, and 11bis requires individual training certificates. These must not be dismissed merely because the scheme uses a different form.

However, the visa text excepts small-scale work and nondestructive outdoor roof/wall asbestos-cement removal when the building is not publicly occupied. Small-scale work expressly includes removal. The capacity-before-visa rule does not on its face impose a separate prior company authorisation in these excepted cases. Individual training certificates do not by themselves establish prior undertaking permission based on both exposure-control and training evidence.

The fresh full authentic May 2026 amender does not amend principal Article 11, so does not itself remove its visa exceptions. Article 14 substitutes the more general permission/list rule, but Article 25 defers it until 1 May 2027. This supports the residual beyond merely missing a special statutory form.

records.conclusion: TARGET is a genuine binding non-bank admission route and indirect SNCE access has substantial safeguards. They do not establish equivalent eligibility and direct-access protection across designated Spanish systems. Fresh SNCE basic rules and current operator admission criteria identify a concrete non-TARGET residual tied to the still-narrow statutory definition.
legalResult: Fresh EU 2024/886 Article 3(2) deletes the designated-system exemption from PSD2 Article 35(1), preserving only the same-group exception; Article 4 expands SFD institution categories; Article 5 requires national implementation by 9 April 2025. The result is qualified eligibility and objective/proportionate/nondiscriminatory access, not guaranteed admission regardless of risk.

Law 41/1999 Article 2(c)(2) still limits the ordinary institution category to credit/investment and specified public/equivalent entities. Its reference to Directive 98/26 Article 2(b) appears within the credit/investment description, not an unqualified dynamic incorporation of every newly added institution. Other participants can qualify in distinct clearing/settlement roles, but no universal ordinary PI/EMI route was established.

Royal Decree-law 19/2018 Article 8(2)(a) still excludes designated systems from the general direct-access safeguards. The same provision gives indirect-access safeguards; these are real protections and must remain prominent.

TARGET conditions published in the authentic September 2025 Banco de España resolution add non-bank eligibility and safeguards. This is binding operational implementation, not mere guidance. The later May 2026 rule does not repeal that route. It is system-specific and does not amend other designated systems or their statutory protections.

Fresh SNCE basic regulation, published in BOE in February 2024 with Banco de España approval, makes ordinary membership depend on Law 41/1999 eligibility (Article 5), permits reasoned refusal for failure of statutory eligibility (Article 6), and expressly says an accessible nonmember is not a member (Article 23(6)). Its objective/non-discriminatory accessible-entity protection (23(7)) concerns the indirect route.

The operator Iberpay current adhesion page explicitly limits participants/direct settlement to EEA credit institutions and links to Law 41/1999 while listing 2026 admission windows. This corroborates an operative general eligibility distinction outside TARGET, beyond mere absence of the new national statutory form. It does not prove an actual refusal or exclude overriding EU protection.
